title: THE BIBLE TALKS ABOUT RAPE, MENSTRUATION, PROSTITUTION, VIRGINITY, POLYGAMY, AND DIVORCE—BUT THE TRUTH HIDING IN THESE PASSAGES MAY CHANGE HOW YOU SEE GOD FOREVER
paragraphs: THE BIBLE TALKS ABOUT RAPE, MENSTRUATION, PROSTITUTION, VIRGINITY, POLYGAMY, AND DIVORCE—BUT THE TRUTH HIDING IN THESE PASSAGES MAY CHANGE HOW YOU SEE GOD FOREVER

They told you the Bible was a book of rules about sex, purity, marriage, and shame. But what if some of its most uncomfortable passages reveal a God who sees the violated, defends the vulnerable, confronts the powerful, and refuses to reduce a human being to what happened to their body?
There is a woman sitting in a church somewhere who has never told anyone what happened to her.
She sings during worship. She smiles when someone asks how she is doing. She knows the right words to say when the pastor talks about forgiveness.
But every time someone mentions purity, something inside her tightens.
Because years ago, someone took something from her without her consent.
And ever since, she has wondered whether God looks at her differently.
There is another woman who has been divorced, who feels every sermon about marriage is somehow aimed at her.
There is a young man fighting sexual temptation who believes his repeated failures have made him permanently unacceptable to God.
There is a wife who has been told that submission means enduring whatever her husband demands.
There is a girl who was taught that menstruation makes her spiritually unclean.
There is a person who has survived sexual exploitation and wonders whether the word prostitute will always be more powerful than the word beloved.
And there are countless believers who have quietly wondered something they are almost afraid to say aloud.
If God is good, why does the Bible contain so many disturbing stories and difficult laws about sex, women, marriage, and human bodies?
That question deserves more than a religious slogan.
It deserves Scripture read carefully, honestly, and in context.
Because there is something extraordinary waiting beneath these difficult passages.
Not every biblical law describes God's ideal. Not every action recorded in Scripture carries God's approval. Not every ancient cultural practice should be reproduced by Christians today.
And perhaps most importantly, the Bible does not ask us to confuse what sinful human beings have done with what the Creator intended.
To understand the difference, we must go back to the beginning.
Before there was a violated woman, an abandoned spouse, a purchased body, a broken marriage, or a wounded conscience, there was a declaration.
Genesis 1:27 says:
"So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them." (KJV)
The Hebrew expression is בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים — betselem Elohim.
It means "in the image of God."
Not in the image of usefulness.
Not in the image of sexual attractiveness.
Not in the image of marital status.
Not in the image of virginity.
Not in the image of social respectability.
In the image of God.

The Hebrew word tselem refers to an image or representation. In Genesis, it identifies humanity's extraordinary relationship to its Creator and the dignity and responsibility that come with being made in His image.
A woman's dignity does not begin when she marries.
A man's dignity does not disappear when he struggles.
A survivor's dignity is not destroyed by an offender's violence.
And a human being does not become more valuable to God because society considers them sexually respectable.
Before humanity had a sexual history, humanity had a God-given dignity.
That is where the conversation must begin.
And it changes everything that follows.
Consider one of the Bible's most painful accounts.
In 2 Samuel 13, Tamar is assaulted by her half-brother Amnon.
This is not a romantic misunderstanding. It is not seduction. It is not a story about a woman failing to protect her purity.
The text records Tamar's resistance.
"Nay, my brother, do not force me." (2 Samuel 13:12, KJV)
The Hebrew verb עָנָה — anah, used in this account, can describe affliction, humiliation, or violation, depending on context. Here, the narrative makes the sexual violence unmistakable.
Tamar refuses.
Amnon overpowers her.
Then, after committing the assault, he rejects her.
The same man who claimed to desire her suddenly treats her as disposable.
And the Bible does not disguise the cruelty.
It exposes it.
Tamar's brother Absalom takes her into his home, but the narrative leaves us with the devastating image of a woman living in desolation.
What makes this story even more heartbreaking is the failure of those with power.
King David becomes angry, yet the narrative does not record him bringing Tamar the justice she deserves.
The royal household becomes a place where a victim's suffering is entangled with family loyalty, silence, and political consequences.
Does any of that sound painfully familiar?
A respected family.
A powerful offender.
A victim who spoke.
A community more concerned about the scandal than the wounded person.
The Bible recorded this darkness thousands of years before modern conversations about sexual abuse.
But recording an atrocity is not endorsing it.
Tamar's story is not evidence that God approved of her suffering. It is evidence that Scripture is willing to expose the wickedness people would rather conceal.
And if you are reading this with a memory you have never been able to explain, hear this clearly.
What someone did to you was not your sin.
Your resistance did not have to be perfect for the assault to be wrong.
Your worth was not stolen.
You do not owe your abuser access, silence, or reconciliation without repentance and safety.
Forgiveness, when understood biblically, does not require pretending that evil was harmless. It does not cancel accountability, justice, or the need for protection.
The God who commands justice does not ask victims to call oppression love.
Deuteronomy 22:25–27 is especially significant here.

In its ancient legal setting, the passage distinguishes a sexual assault from consensual wrongdoing. It assigns guilt to the attacker and explicitly says that the assaulted woman has committed no offense deserving death.
The passage compares the assault to a man attacking and murdering his neighbor.
That comparison is staggering.
The text recognizes the seriousness of sexual violence and the innocence of the victim.
Yet we must also be honest about another difficult passage.

Deuteronomy 22:28–29 describes a situation involving a man who seizes an unmarried young woman who is not betrothed, followed by a requirement involving payment and marriage. The precise interpretation of the Hebrew wording, including whether this case describes rape or another form of illicit sexual intercourse, is disputed among scholars.
We should not conceal that difficulty.
Nor should we turn an ancient Israelite legal provision into a modern command that a rape survivor must marry her attacker.
That would ignore the historical covenant setting, the complexities of the text, and the broader biblical concern for justice.
Scripture must be interpreted faithfully, not weaponized against the wounded.
And that distinction matters far beyond sexual assault.
Because another misunderstood biblical subject has caused generations of women unnecessary shame.
Menstruation.
Leviticus 15 describes a woman's menstrual bleeding as a condition of ritual impurity.
The Hebrew term is נִדָּה — niddah, associated in this context with menstruation and ritual separation.
But here is what many people were never taught.
Ritual impurity in the Mosaic Law was not automatically moral guilt.

The Old Testament distinguishes between ceremonial conditions and sinful actions. Bodily discharges, childbirth, contact with death, and other ordinary experiences could affect ritual status without making the person morally wicked.
A woman's menstrual cycle was not proof that she was disgusting to God.
It was part of a system governing ritual access to Israel's sanctuary.
The distinction is essential.
And then Jesus enters the story.
Mark 5 tells us about a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years.
Twelve years.
Imagine the exhaustion.
The physical suffering.
The money spent seeking treatment.
The disappointment of hoping this time something might finally work.
The Gospel says she had suffered much under many physicians, had spent what she possessed, and had grown worse.
Then she hears about Jesus.
She approaches Him in the crowd and touches His garment.
And the bleeding stops.
But the miracle is not finished.
Jesus asks who touched Him.
The woman comes forward, trembling.
And instead of publicly humiliating her, He speaks words that restore her dignity.
"Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague." (Mark 5:34, KJV)
Daughter.
Not nuisance.
Not disgrace.
Not a contaminating presence.
Daughter.
The Greek word is θυγάτηρ — thygatēr.
It means "daughter."
Jesus addresses her with a word of personal recognition and tenderness.
The passage does not mean that every sick person who has enough faith will be physically healed. Nor does it mean that all suffering is caused by sin.
It reveals something about the character of Christ.
He does not treat a suffering woman as someone beneath His attention.
He stops.
He listens.
He speaks peace.
And suddenly the question becomes painfully personal.
How many people have been made to feel unworthy in religious spaces when the Savior Himself was willing to stop for someone the crowd barely noticed?
Now consider prostitution.
Few subjects reveal the difference between religious reputation and divine mercy as powerfully as this one.
In Joshua 2, we encounter Rahab.
She is identified as a prostitute.
The Hebrew word is זוֹנָה — zonah, commonly meaning a prostitute.
Scripture does not erase that description.
But neither does it allow that description to be the final word about her.
Rahab recognizes the power of Israel's God and protects the Israelite spies. Her actions become part of the story of Jericho's fall and her household's deliverance.
Hebrews 11:31 remembers her faith.
James 2:25 remembers her actions.
And Matthew 1:5 includes Rahab in the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Read that again.
A woman introduced in the Old Testament by a socially stigmatized occupation appears in the recorded ancestry of the Messiah.
This does not mean prostitution is celebrated as God's design.

Sexual exploitation, economic desperation, coercion, and the buying and selling of sexual access are serious matters. Scripture's sexual ethic cannot be reduced to either blanket condemnation of vulnerable people or approval of exploitation.
Rahab's story makes a different point.
A person's past does not place them beyond the reach of God's redemptive purposes.
And the Gospel carries that truth further.
In John 8:1–11, a woman accused of adultery is brought before Jesus.
The religious accusers want judgment.
Jesus exposes their hypocrisy.
Then He tells the woman:
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." (John 8:11, KJV)

There is an important textual detail: this passage is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John, and its placement varies in the manuscript tradition. It should therefore be discussed with that qualification rather than presented as an undisputed part of John's earliest recoverable text.
Nevertheless, the themes of mercy, repentance, and Christ's authority are firmly established elsewhere in the New Testament.
John 3:17 says that God sent His Son not to condemn the world, but that the world through Him might be saved.
Romans 2:4 teaches that God's goodness leads toward repentance.
And 1 Corinthians 6:11 speaks of people whose former sins did not define their final standing before God because they were washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of Jesus Christ.
Grace is not permission to continue destroying ourselves or others.
Grace is God's undeserved favor that brings forgiveness and calls us into a transformed life.
Jesus does not need to pretend our sin is harmless in order to prove His mercy is real.
That brings us to another subject that has been used to measure human value.
Virginity.
In the ancient biblical world, virginity carried significant social and marital implications, particularly for women.
The Hebrew בְּתוּלָה — betulah commonly refers to a virgin or young woman understood to be sexually inexperienced, though interpretation in individual passages depends on context.
The Greek παρθένος — parthenos likewise commonly means "virgin," although its range of usage requires attention to context.
Scripture treats sexual faithfulness seriously.
Jesus teaches against lustful objectification in Matthew 5:27–28.
Paul calls believers to flee sexual immorality in 1 Corinthians 6:18.
And Hebrews 13:4 honors marriage and marital fidelity.
But there is a dangerous distortion that must be confronted.
Sexual purity is not a currency with which people purchase human worth.
Virginity is not the image of God.
A person who has been sexually assaulted has not committed sexual sin by being assaulted.
A believer who has sinned sexually is not beyond forgiveness.
And a person who has remained sexually abstinent has no reason to boast as though holiness were a personal achievement independent of God's grace.
The Gospel calls us to chastity, faithfulness, repentance, and self-control.
But it never teaches that a human being becomes worthless after sexual sin.
Listen to Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 6:11:
"And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God."
Some of you.
Were.
But.
Those words carry the weight of redemption.
The Greek verb ἀπελούσασθε — apelousasthe, translated "ye are washed" in the KJV, conveys washing or cleansing.
Paul is not saying that the Corinthians had never sinned.
He is saying that their former lives did not have the final authority to define them.
That is the power of the Gospel.
It does not rewrite history by denying what happened.
It changes the sinner's standing before God through Christ.
And when the discussion turns to marriage, the Bible becomes even more challenging.
Because some people have been taught that marriage gives one spouse unrestricted rights over the other's body.
But listen to the surprising mutuality of 1 Corinthians 7:3–4.
Paul speaks about the marital obligations of husband and wife, then says:
"The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband: and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife." (1 Corinthians 7:4, KJV)
The Greek verb associated with authority here is ἐξουσιάζει — exousiazei, from exousiazō, meaning to exercise authority over.
Notice the reciprocity.
Paul does not give only the husband a claim.
He speaks of mutual marital responsibilities.
And verse 5 speaks of abstaining by mutual agreement for a time.
These verses have sometimes been misused to justify sexual coercion.
But that reading ignores the broader New Testament command to love sacrificially, honor one another, and reject harshness and abuse.
Ephesians 5:25 commands husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for it.
Colossians 3:19 commands husbands not to be bitter or harsh toward their wives.
First Peter 3:7 calls husbands to treat their wives with honor.
Marriage does not turn a person into property.
Marital intimacy is not a biblical excuse for intimidation, violence, or forced sexual acts.
A wedding covenant does not erase the dignity, safety, or personhood of either spouse.
And a husband cannot claim to imitate the self-giving love of Christ while using fear to control his wife.
The cross reveals love that gives itself for another.
Not love that destroys another to satisfy itself.
But what about polygamy?
Abraham had Sarah and Hagar.
Jacob had Leah and Rachel, along with Bilhah and Zilpah.
David had multiple wives.
Solomon had many wives and concubines.
If the Bible records these arrangements, does that mean God designed marriage to work that way?
Here we must distinguish between description and prescription.
Genesis 2:24 presents the foundational marriage pattern:
"Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh."
The Hebrew phrase בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad means "one flesh."
It describes a profound union.
The biblical narratives involving polygamy repeatedly show jealousy, rivalry, favoritism, fractured households, and spiritual consequences.
Sarah and Hagar's relationship becomes deeply painful.
Leah and Rachel struggle within a divided household.
Solomon's many marriages contribute to his turning away from the Lord, as 1 Kings 11 records.
Yet the Mosaic Law also regulated situations involving multiple wives.
Exodus 21:10, for example, addresses a woman's rights to food, clothing, and marital obligations if a man takes another wife.
That law is significant because it recognizes obligations owed to a vulnerable woman within an existing social arrangement.
But regulating a practice does not necessarily establish it as God's original ideal.
Jesus makes this interpretive principle especially clear when discussing divorce.
In Matthew 19, the Pharisees question Him about whether a man may divorce his wife for any reason.
Jesus directs them back to Genesis.
He quotes the creation account and says:
"What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder." (Matthew 19:6, KJV)
When they ask why Moses permitted divorce, Jesus responds:
"Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so." (Matthew 19:8, KJV)
There it is.
One of the most important interpretive statements in the entire conversation.
"From the beginning it was not so."
Jesus distinguishes between an accommodation within a fallen human society and the Creator's intention from the beginning.
Not everything tolerated or regulated under ancient Israel's civil law expresses the fullness of God's design.
The Bible is not merely a collection of isolated regulations.
It tells a developing story of creation, human rebellion, covenant, judgment, mercy, and redemption, reaching its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
And that brings us to divorce.
Perhaps you have lived through one.
Perhaps you are still grieving a marriage that ended.
Perhaps you were abandoned.
Perhaps you were betrayed.
Perhaps you stayed far longer than anyone knows because you believed leaving would mean disappointing God.
Or perhaps you were the one who sinned, and you now carry the consequences of choices you deeply regret.
The Bible does not treat divorce casually.
Malachi 2 condemns marital treachery.
Jesus challenges the casual dismissal of spouses.
Paul addresses marriage, separation, and abandonment in 1 Corinthians 7.
Christians have long differed over the precise grounds for divorce and remarriage, particularly regarding sexual immorality in Matthew 19:9 and abandonment in 1 Corinthians 7:15.
These disagreements should not be hidden.
But neither should the seriousness of marriage become an excuse to dismiss abuse.

A person facing violence or coercion needs protection, wise support, and practical safety. Churches should not demand that endangered spouses remain exposed to harm while theological questions are being worked through.
Marriage is holy.
So is the human life within it.
And no faithful reading of Scripture should require us to pretend that cruelty is covenant faithfulness.
God's design for marriage is not the preservation of a respectable appearance at the cost of a person's destruction.
It is a covenant intended to reflect faithfulness, love, mutual honor, and responsibility.
When that covenant is shattered, the suffering deserves to be taken seriously.
And when people repent of wrongdoing, grace offers a genuine path toward transformation without erasing consequences or accountability.
Now stand back and look at everything we have encountered.
Tamar, whose voice was ignored.
The bleeding woman, whom Jesus called daughter.
Rahab, whose story became part of the Messiah's genealogy.
The unmarried person, whose worth is not measured by sexual history.
The married couple, called to mutual honor rather than domination.
The households fractured by polygamy.
The spouses wounded by betrayal and divorce.
These are not merely disconnected controversies about sex.
They reveal the devastating consequences of treating human beings as objects of possession, appetite, control, reputation, or convenience.
And against that darkness stands the declaration of Genesis.
Made in God's image.
And then the person of Jesus Christ.
The One who touched lepers.
The One who welcomed the despised.
The One who exposed religious hypocrisy.
The One who called sinners to repentance.
The One who defended the vulnerable without pretending sin was good.
The One who gave His life for people who could never purchase their own redemption.
In John 1:14, we read:
"And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us."
The Greek is Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο — Kai ho logos sarx egeneto.
"And the Word became flesh."
Think about that.
The eternal Son of God entered embodied human existence.
He was not ashamed to become truly human.
He experienced hunger.
Exhaustion.
Grief.
Pain.
He was betrayed.
Stripped.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
The sinless Savior endured public humiliation and bodily violence at the hands of sinners.
Yet He did not become less holy because others treated Him shamefully.
And in His resurrection, He did not abandon the human body as something worthless.
He rose bodily, gloriously victorious over death.
Christian hope is not that our bodies never mattered.
It is that the Creator intends to redeem His people completely.
Body and soul.
That is why Christian sexual ethics cannot be reduced to fear, control, or reputation management.
Our bodies matter because God made us.
Our choices matter because holiness matters.
Our neighbors matter because they bear God's image.
Our wounds matter because God is compassionate.
And our sins matter because they required the saving work of Christ.
But listen carefully.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction brings sin into the light so that repentance and healing can begin.
Condemnation tells you there is no hope.
The Gospel says otherwise.
Romans 8:1 declares:
"There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus."
Not because sin was imaginary.
Not because evil had no consequences.
But because Jesus Christ bore the judgment due to sinners and opened the way to reconciliation with God.
He was crucified.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith receives the promise of forgiveness and new life.
That is not religious self-improvement.
That is redemption.
Perhaps the most difficult thing about reading these biblical passages is that they force us to confront what we have done with God's gift of human dignity.
We have used purity to shame victims.
Used marriage to excuse control.
Used religion to silence the wounded.
Used grace to avoid accountability.
Used the language of love to conceal lust.
Used Scripture selectively to defend the powerful.
And sometimes, in our determination to win arguments about morality, we have forgotten the human beings sitting in front of us.
The woman who flinches when someone raises their voice.
The man who has never confessed the addiction consuming his private life.
The teenager who thinks one sexual mistake has ruined the rest of their future.
The spouse who cries quietly after everyone else has gone to sleep.
The believer who knows the Bible's commands but has forgotten that the Savior who gives those commands is also merciful.
What if the Church became a place where truth was never sacrificed, but wounded people were never treated as disposable?
Where repentance was preached without humiliating victims.
Where sexual holiness was taught without reducing people to their sexual past.
Where marriage was honored without concealing abuse.
Where forgiveness was proclaimed without denying justice.
Where grace was celebrated without making excuses for sin.
And where Jesus Christ, not public reputation, remained at the center.
That would not mean abandoning biblical conviction.
It would mean taking biblical conviction seriously enough to apply it to everyone.
To the victim and the offender, while never confusing their moral responsibility.
To the husband and the wife.
To the pastor and the congregation.
To the wealthy and the poor.
To the respectable and the disgraced.
Because the cross leaves no room for self-righteous superiority.
And the resurrection leaves no room for believing that sin and shame must have the final word.
Maybe you have reached this point and realized that your deepest struggle is not with an ancient passage.
It is with your own story.
Something you did.
Something someone did to you.
A marriage that broke.
A secret you have hidden.
A wound you have mistaken for your identity.
A sin you have justified.
A burden you have carried so long that you no longer remember what peace feels like.
Do not confuse those things.
If you were violated, you need not repent for another person's violence.
If you have violated someone else, genuine repentance requires truth, accountability, and a decisive turning away from harm.
If you are trapped in sexual sin, grace does not tell you to surrender to it.
If you are wounded, grace does not demand that you pretend you are healed.
Jesus meets people truthfully.
And He calls them toward life.
You can begin by speaking to Him without performance.

Lord Jesus, You know what happened. You know what I have done and what has been done to me. Show me what I need to confess, what I need to release, where I need protection, and where I need healing. Teach me to receive Your grace and walk in Your truth. Amen.
And if you are struggling, you do not have to turn your pain into a public testimony before you are ready. Find a trustworthy, safe person who can listen, pray, and help you take the next wise step.
There is no spiritual virtue in exposing private trauma to strangers.
But there is profound courage in refusing to let shame isolate you forever.
If this article has touched something deep inside you, I want to invite you into a conversation that matters.
And if you have experienced the restoring mercy of Jesus, consider sharing a few words of your testimony. Someone else may be reading silently, wondering whether redemption is possible for them too.
You do not need to disclose anything unsafe or deeply private.
Sometimes the simplest confession of faith is the one another person most needs to hear.
And please do not let this message end with you.
Not because difficult biblical conversations are comfortable.
But because someone you know may be carrying shame that was never theirs to carry.
Send this to a believer who has struggled to reconcile the Bible's difficult passages with the goodness of God.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who have walked away from faith to follow as well.
Because this mission is not about building an audience around scandal.
It is about pointing people from scandal to grace.
And that brings me to something personal about the work we are building together.
Gospel Warrior exists to help people encounter biblical truth, grow in spiritual maturity, and discover the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
Resources intended to help believers read Scripture more carefully.
Understand the Gospel more deeply.
Grow in prayer.
Strengthen their families.
Resist temptation.
Find biblical encouragement.
And become disciples who are rooted in Christ rather than carried away by every passing opinion.
But continuing and expanding this work requires real support.
Research, writing, resource development, distribution, and the ongoing work of reaching people all involve time, effort, and expense.
Not because God measures your devotion by whether you pay for an online ministry.
And not because giving money can purchase spiritual favor.
Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ. It cannot be bought.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
The Greek word ἱλαρόν — hilaron, translated "cheerful," describes willing, joyful generosity.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Not manipulation.
A willing heart.
You may prayerfully choose to include that support within your personal giving budget, alongside your responsibilities to your local church, family, and others in need.
These are not merely items to purchase.
A book can become a doorway into deeper study.
A journal can become a place where someone writes prayers they have never spoken aloud.
A shirt can become the beginning of a conversation about Jesus.
And a simple gift can remind someone that they are seen, loved, and invited to grow in faith.
It is the opportunity to help make biblically grounded encouragement and discipleship resources available to more people.
Pray for this ministry.
Use the free resources.
Encourage others to study the Word of God for themselves.
Because the Gospel is not a product.
Jesus Christ is not for sale.
The mission is to make His truth known.
Before you leave, return to the question that brought us here.
Why does the Bible talk about sexual assault, menstruation, prostitution, virginity, marital rights, polygamy, and divorce?
Because the Bible speaks to real human life.
Not a sanitized world.
Not a world without betrayal.
Not a world where everyone gets married, stays faithful, and lives without regret.
It speaks to the world we actually inhabit.
A world where bodies are wounded.
Where promises are broken.
Where people exploit one another.
Where shame spreads.
Where religious leaders sometimes fail.
Where sinners need repentance.
Where victims need justice.
Where marriages need faithfulness.
Where the lonely need compassion.
And where every one of us needs a Savior.
The Bible does not flatten all these experiences into one moral category.
It distinguishes sin from suffering, covenant from coercion, purity from ritual status, justice from revenge, and grace from permission to continue in evil.

And when we read these passages through the larger story of Scripture, culminating in Jesus Christ, we encounter a God who created humanity with dignity, commands righteousness, confronts injustice, and offers redemption through His Son.
The Christian story begins with human beings made in God's image.
It reaches its decisive turning point at the cross and empty tomb.
And it looks forward to the day when God will make all things new.
Revelation 21:4 promises that God will wipe away every tear and that death, sorrow, crying, and pain will not endure forever.
That promise does not make today's suffering insignificant.
It tells us that suffering will not have the final word.
So to the person who has been violated, you are not what your attacker did.
To the person who has sinned, you are not beyond the reach of repentance and forgiveness.
To the person grieving a broken marriage, your story has not ceased to matter.
To the person who has been treated as disposable, you bear the image of the living God.
And to every believer who has confused religious respectability with righteousness, remember that we all stand in need of grace.
There is only one Savior.
His name is Jesus.
He is not embarrassed by the truth about the human condition.
He came to redeem sinners.
He calls us to holiness.
He teaches us to love our neighbors.
He commands us to protect the vulnerable and practice justice.
He offers forgiveness to the repentant.
And He gives eternal life to those who trust in Him.
The world may remember the scandal.
The crowd may remember the accusation.
The offender may have tried to write your story in pain.
Your own sin may have left consequences you cannot simply undo.
But neither another person's cruelty nor your own repentant past has the authority to declare God's grace powerless.
The chapter that broke your heart does not have to be the chapter that buries your hope—because the hands that were pierced for sinners still belong to the risen Savior.
